question: An operations lead argues that because most Message Batches finish processing in under an hour, the team can safely promise customers a fixed 90-minute turnaround for a nightly summarization job. A colleague pushes back on this plan. What is the strongest technical objection to the promise?
options: A) Summarization requests inherently take longer to process than other request types, so 90 minutes is too short a window regardless of typical batch completion times
B) The Batches API caps total daily throughput per workspace, so a 90-minute promise would only be broken once the workspace exceeds its allotted request volume
C) The Batches API carries no guaranteed latency SLA, so a batch can legitimately take up to 24 hours under heavy demand, making a fixed 90-minute promise unreliable
D) Fixed turnaround promises are incompatible with the Batches API because every batch must be manually retrieved through the console rather than through automated polling
correct_answers: C) The Batches API carries no guaranteed latency SLA, so a batch can legitimately take up to 24 hours under heavy demand, making a fixed 90-minute promise unreliable
explanations: Incorrect. Summarization is not documented as a request type with inherently longer processing times than other Messages API workloads within a batch.
Incorrect. The objection to a fixed-time promise is the lack of an SLA, not a workspace-level daily throughput cap being the mechanism that would break it.

Correct. Typical fast completion is not a guarantee; the Batches API can take up to its full 24-hour window when demand is high, so committing to a fixed 90-minute SLA misrepresents the platform's actual guarantee.
Incorrect. Batch results can be retrieved programmatically through the retrieval endpoint and are not limited to manual console access, so this is not the relevant risk to the promise.
